text.en: In the villages of Anand district in Gujarat, farmers used to cycle or walk to nearby villages to sell milk in the scorching heat. If the milk spoiled, it was lost, and middlemen bought it cheaply. Then the farmers formed a cooperative and today their milk becomes butter, ghee and milk powder sold across India. This story shows how different kinds of work depend on each other.

As societies progressed, the number of economic activities by which people earn a living grew. They are grouped into three main sectors: primary, secondary and tertiary. The primary sector involves taking raw materials directly from nature, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining. The secondary sector turns raw materials from the primary sector into products for sale. It includes making flour in mills, extracting oil from groundnuts, processing tea leaves, constructing buildings and roads and providing utilities like water, electricity and gas. The tertiary sector provides services: doctors, nurses, teachers, lawyers, pilots, drivers, shopkeepers and bankers help others. It supports the other two sectors and adds to the prosperity of a nation.
Farmers in Anand had to sell their milk quickly before it spoiled, so they depended on middlemen, who bought milk in bulk at low prices and sold it in the market. Under the guidance of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, farmers formed a cooperative, a group of people who work together for a common aim, and they collected, processed and sold the milk themselves. AMUL, Anand Milk Union Limited, was set up in 1946 under the leadership of Tribhuvandas Patel, a lawyer and freedom fighter, and Dr Varghese Kurien, an engineer. It brought farmers, including women, together and gave them control over production and sale. At the end of the month they are paid for the milk according to its quantity and quality. They set up a factory in Anand to make butter, ghee, cheese and milk powder. Milk is pasteurised, which means heated to a specific temperature to make it safe, and then transported to shops in towns, cities and villages across India.
In the AMUL story the farmers who keep cows and milk them work in the primary sector. The factory that turns milk into butter and milk powder is in the secondary sector. Transport, retail shops and distribution are in the tertiary sector. The books you study go through the same chain: trees (primary), paper and printing (secondary), and the shop and delivery (tertiary). Used paper can also be recycled, and recycling paper takes about 70 percent less energy and water than making new paper from wood pulp. Goods and services from one country may be sold in another country. Such goods are called exports. Every sector depends on the others, so the economic activities in a neighbourhood form a connected web.

problem.en: Classify as primary, secondary or tertiary: a fisherman, a flour mill worker, a bank clerk, a tea picker.

text.en: A fisherman and a tea picker take things from nature: primary.
A flour mill worker changes grain into flour: secondary.
A bank clerk provides a service: tertiary.

problem.en: Trace the sectors in the making of a cotton shirt.

text.en: Farmers grow cotton: primary.
Mills spin yarn and weave cloth and a factory stitches the shirt: secondary.
A shop sells the shirt: tertiary.

prompt.en: How do the three sectors depend on each other? Use AMUL as an example.

requiredIdeas.en: Factories make butter and milk powder (secondary).

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking only farming is an economic activity.

points.en: The three sectors are primary, secondary and tertiary.
The primary sector takes raw materials from nature, the secondary changes them into products, and the tertiary gives services.
AMUL shows how a cooperative links all three.
